With my hardware setup and very rough knowledge of chemistry, the best I'm doing is to tune the holos bandwith within a few tens of nanometers.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
I've made many reflection H2s (mostly from transmission H1s) for use with laser light for contact copying, in AgX and DCG. With AgX, bandwidth is about 30nm (narrow) so the processing needs to be ultra-smooth so you don't see squeege or other processing marks. With DCG, the bandwidth should (I think) be as narrow as the coating and drying uniformity will allow. 

Dave points out that, with laser irradiation, a narrow bandwidth reflection hologram will have more of its modulation available for the image at a specific wavelength. This means it will either have higher diffraction efficiency (though possibly look dimmer) or have higher signal-to-noise ratio. Both of these are attributes of a good reflection "intermaster" or "production tool" hologram.

Dave, I don't think your model is right here. It's not true that a broadband hologram necessarily has a lower diffraction efficiency. In principle you could have a broadband hologram that is 100% efficient in a broad band of wavelengths. So you could have a narrowband hologram and a very broadband one, and under laser illumination they would look identical.

As an addendum to my last comment, I see a lot of opinion being thrown around.

One way to settle things is to measure the DE. Shoot a laser beam through your holograms and measure the relative DE between your narrow and broad band holograms. Post the results.

If you measure the DE on as many as possible you'll limit the margin of error introduced by differing emulsion batches and processing experiments.

Just going by eye isn't going to give you objective results that can be supported.

OK, I think the main issue here is the definition of narrow band and broad band which I pointed out and is in the opening post in this thread. When I think of narrow band I am thinking of making a reflection hologram with 514 and it does not replay in 532. I stated that broadband does not mean a white hologram.

Now, I have made some very narrow band, I know this because the hologram is nicely bright in white light but does not replay in the wavelength I shot it in. It has not shifted as far as the eye can see, color wise. And when put in the laser light parts of the image dissapear and reappear as you change the illluminating laser light angle. This to me says two things. First the hologram is narrow band. If it was broad band then the whole image would be visible at the same time at some angle, second the bragg planes have not swollen and dried uniformly. Some are replaying 514, some 517, some 520 etc.. Thus the reason parts of the image are viewable at slightly different angles.

Now back to the point I was trying to make. If you process the reflection hologram such that it replays from ( I think I stated 20 - 30nm swing) 494 to 534 nm, then it is much easier (the key word here is easier and I will expain why in a minute) to produce a usable master. As I stated it is much easier, for me anyway, to produce a non narrow band hologram on the first try then trying to produce one that is narrow band and then reprocess it to tune it to my wavelengh. Sometime this takes a few reprocessings. Of which then I can figure out exactly time, temp etc with the current envionmental factors works. Too many reprocessings are not good so after the narrow band replay is found, I need to make another hologram using the parameters I have found to work. This is a lot more trouble then simply slightly warming the alcohols or if they are cool, do a quicker alcohol dry to get a more forgiving reflection master.

To support this, and this is whom I was originally speaking to in the original thread that this thread branch off of, Cristiano replied that he found it easier to do the same. So you see, two persons found the same results.

I mentioned that Dave must have a great system to consistantly be able to produce narrow band holograms tuned to the recording wavelength. And I truely meant it when I said it. 

The reason I asked Dave to show his narrow band hologram is to see if it was actually narrow band. I still don't believe it is. I can't tell from the first video (the camera bleaches out the hologram), but I will take his word for it. In his second video the hologram turns yellow at one angle. Is this normal for a narrow band reflection hologram? I would have thought the image to just disappear if the hologram was narrow band at the extreem angles. How can it be replaying yellow if it is truely narrow band. Maybe it is I who is missing something. Or again, maybe it is the camera.
